p: Gene Vigil turned out to be the detective who stood in Dani's basement when she was fifteen and asked who did the laundry.
His 2007 notebook held two things nobody ever followed: the word cap, written down and struck through, and the word boy, with a question mark, in the margin.
Ana's own story of a bar fight on Colfax broke his rule about bar fights, and Dani moved her test from January to June.
On her second visit Gene gave her the notebook in a freezer bag, for Ana. He told her that on the night of the arrest, her father asked him one thing: was anybody else hurt.
In her car afterward Dani counted her family that night. There wasn't anybody else.
Ana Brennan. Gene's notebook sits on her desk, zipped in its bag.
Ronnie Galvan. The bartender at the Night Owl Tap in 2007. He runs a taqueria in Commerce City now.
Gene Vigil. The retired detective, out in Northglenn.
Luis Ruiz. Still playing Dani by phone, a move a call.
Teo Ruiz. The one who gets the call when something breaks at the house.
Lupe Ruiz. For Christmas her grandfather mailed her a pencil drawing of a knight.

Saturday, January 16. Gene Vigil's notebook lived on the corner of Ana's desk now, still in its freezer bag. Ana had read it three times that week, and after every reading she zipped the bag shut, the whole length of the seal, slowly, as if Gene could see her from Northglenn.

Twenty one weeks to June. Dani had started timing herself after New Year's: one full Logical Reasoning section on Sunday mornings, thirty five minutes on her phone, at the kitchen table under the photo on the fridge. Last Sunday she'd finished with four minutes to spare and missed six. Ana had asked to see the six. Ana always asked to see the wrong ones.

We're going to file in March, Ana said. It goes to the DA in Brighton, and it lands on Meredith Sloane's desk. Chief deputy. She's the best they have, and she's fair, which is worse. She'll read every line we write looking for the soft spot. She tapped the pencil on the freezer bag. So before she does, we weigh things.

Phil's box was open on the floor. Ana had pulled three sheets out of it and laid them side by side: a handwritten statement taken the night of the fight, a page from the March 2008 hearing, and a page from the trial. The same name on all three. Ronald Galvan.
Everybody in this case saw a jacket, Ana said. Consuelo saw a jacket. You saw a jacket. The lab saw blood on a jacket. Ronnie Galvan is the only witness who ever saw your father do anything.

Dani knew what he'd said. She'd read it in the transcript years ago, and she'd decided then what to do with it. Pa said everybody was shoving. A bartender pouring four deep for a bar full of Boston fans saw what he saw. She'd put it in a drawer in her head and shut the drawer.
Dicta got up off the rug, turned around once, and lay back down facing the other way, which was as much as she ever said about anything.

The whiteboard hadn't changed since December. The long sentence across the top, the line under it, the four lines under that. Line two, SOME OF THE BLOOD CAME FROM THE ATTACK, NOT THE BAR. Line four, NEAR THE LOT AT 11:15. Off to the side, nowhere near any of them, CAP and BOY?
Ana wrote under CAP, in pencil this time, not marker. THE MAN WORE A CAP. LUIS NEVER WORE ONE. SO THE MAN WASN'T LUIS.
That's ours, she said. It isn't proof, and it doesn't have to be. It's weight. Give me one fact that, if it turned out true, would put the most weight on it.
That whoever saw him walk out of the bar at 10:45 saw him with nothing on his head.

Ana writes ASK GALVAN on the board, and underlines it. Half an hour before. It doesn't close the gap all the way. A man can find a cap in thirty minutes. But now they need a cap from nowhere, and that's their problem, not ours.

Strengthen. The argument's weak point is the night itself. Seeing him bareheaded thirty minutes before the attack narrows the gap: for the man in the cap to be Luis, he'd have had to put one on between the bar and the curb. It doesn't prove anything. It doesn't have to.

Ana took off her reading glasses and set them on Phil's box, folded. Dani had seen her do that twice: once to play a judge, and once, on the phone, to play her own landlord, who wanted the rent and a reason. Somebody else was coming into the room.

Five minutes. I'm Meredith Sloane. Even her chair creaked different. I've read your cap. I've read your dispatch log, which your side had in 2008 and sat on, thanks. I've got a jury's verdict and a woman across the street who saw red. So go on. What do I say that does your cap the most damage?
Dani had spent eight years guessing what the other side would say, in other people's cases. Never in this one. It took her a second to find the switch.
That a man who means to hurt somebody might put on a hat he'd never wear, so nobody knows him.

Ana, as Meredith, dry as toast: Mr. Ruiz never wore hats, Your Honor. That's exactly why he wore one. Glasses back on. It's a lousy argument, Ana says, herself again. It's also her best, because it doesn't need Consuelo wrong about anything. She borrows our fact and turns it around.

Weaken. The strongest attack gives the cap an explanation that fits Luis: a man hiding who he is wears what he never wears. And it leaves Consuelo's account alone, which matters, since the State needs her eyes for the red.

Monday, January 18, the office was closed for the holiday, and at two thirty Dani was in a booth in a strip mall off Highway 2, four blocks from the vape shop that used to be the Night Owl. The lunch rush was over. A radio in the kitchen, a woman wiping tables, a man's voice back there laughing at something.
She ordered and didn't eat it. She took out the copy Ana had made of the first sheet, the one from the night itself.

Commerce City Police Department, witness statement of Ronald Galvan, taken by Officer D. Archuleta, Saturday, October 27, 2007, at twenty to twelve at night. I'm the bartender at the Night Owl. I was working the bar alone after the game. It was packed, mostly Boston people and the refinery guys. Around ten twenty five I heard yelling over by the hallway to the bathrooms and I looked up. Luis Ruiz, who comes in Saturdays with the Platte Valley crew, swung at a guy I didn't know and hit him in the face. Luis swung first. The other guy came back at him and they were grabbing and shoving. I came over the bar and got between them. The other guy had beer all down his front. Luis's nose was bleeding on his jacket. I told Luis to go home and cool off, and he went out the back about a quarter to eleven. I didn't see the other guy go. I never had trouble with Luis before. I don't know what it was about.
She'd read it before. She read it now as Ana had taught her to read anything a witness wrote: only what he'd stand behind, and nothing she wanted to add.

Two sentences, and they don't fight each other. Luis swung first. I don't know what it was about. He put both down on the same page, twenty minutes before midnight, and he never tried to make one of them bigger than the other.
Would agree with. Both halves are in the statement: "Luis swung first" and "I don't know what it was about," along with "I looked up" at the yelling. He vouches for the punch and nothing before it.
The man in the kitchen came out wiping his hands on a towel over his shoulder. Heavy in the forearms, gray at the temples, reading glasses pushed up on his head. He saw her and stopped walking.

You're Luis's girl, he said. You've got his whole face. He sat down across from her without asking, the towel still on his shoulder. He used to carry your report cards in his wallet. Showed them to the whole bar. You got a B in chemistry once and he wanted to go down to that school and have words with somebody.
She hadn't known that. She didn't know what to do with her face.

I know why you're here. He folded his hands on the table. I'll tell you what I told everybody. I was pulling a pitcher. I heard yelling and I looked up and Luis hit the guy, right in the face. Your dad swung first, Dani. I'm sorry. I'd give a lot for it to be different.
She'd come in with one question, about a hat. She found she had another one first.
You looked up at the yelling. Whatever came before the yelling, you never saw.

He thinks about it. Doesn't look away. That's true. I didn't see what started it. I saw who swung. He turns his coffee cup a little. Something started it. Luis didn't just hit people. It's a dent. It's in the part she didn't come for.

Weaken. Read what he claims: Luis swung first. Then read where he was looking. He looked up at the yelling, so anything before the yelling, a grab, a shove, somebody else's fist, he missed. "First" turns into "first that I saw." He's still good on the punch. He was never good on why.
Once he'd started he kept going. It was a night he'd told too many times and never once all the way to the end.

The guy who died. He'd been on the Boston people since the third inning. Loud. I almost cut him off twice. When the yelling started he had his back to me, bent over some, yelling down at something by the hallway. I couldn't see over the people. He was already wet. Beer all down him. Somebody'd knocked a glass into him, I figured.
Then she asked hers. When Pa went out the back. Was he wearing a hat?
Ronnie actually smiled. Luis? Luis never wore a hat in his life. Said they made him look like his brother. The smile went. No hat. I'd swear to it. Nobody ever asked me that.
She asked about a bar tab. Phil had wanted one in 2008. Ronnie shook his head. Cash bar on a Series night. Nobody ran a tab. I couldn't tell you half the names in there.
I wrote him once, he said, to his coffee. After the trial. He never wrote back. I don't blame him.

She believed him. About the hat, and about the punch. He'd been working that room both times, close enough to break up the one and watch the other go out the back. That was the trouble with having good reasons. They didn't care which side you were on.

Eleven forty at night, the statement says. Travis Hensley died at 1:40. At twenty to twelve there was no murder yet, only a fight and a man on a stretcher. Ronnie said swung first before anybody knew what story they'd need.

Strengthen. An account given before there was any case to fit it to can't have been shaped by the case. The timing rules out the most likely way an honest witness goes wrong: telling the story the investigation later needs.

That night she brushed her teeth at the bathroom sink, the same sink, the same mirror with the silver going at one corner. She'd read grabbing and shoving at the taqueria, and it waited for the mirror, nineteen years deep.

Sunday, October 28, 2007. She'd come home at eight and gone to sleep on the couch. Around noon she'd gotten up to pee, and the bathroom door was open, and her father was shaving. He never shaved on a Sunday. Never. A square of toilet paper was stuck to his neck under his jaw, the left side, with a red dot coming through it. Cut myself, mija. Go back to sleep.

She'd gone back to sleep. Gene came at three. By then it was a nick under his collar, and nobody looks twice at a man who's shaved. He never shaved on Sundays. She'd never once asked herself why he had that one. She'd never told a soul, because there had never been anything to tell.

She sat on the edge of the tub with Ronnie's statement on her knees. The other guy came back at him and they were grabbing and shoving. She went through what she had, one thing at a time, and asked which of them did the most for that sentence.

It could have been a razor. She knows that. But it's the only thing on her list that didn't come out of Ronnie's mouth, and it sits right where a man's hands go when he's grabbing somebody. She doesn't write it down. She doesn't need to.

Strengthen or weaken a passage claim. The statement says the men were grabbing and shoving. A fresh mark on Luis's neck the next morning is independent support for that, from a different source. It fits a shaving cut too, which is why it strengthens rather than proves.
Tuesday, January 19, she told Ana about the hat. She told her about the punch, and about the report cards. She didn't tell her about the bathroom.
Ana listened without writing anything down. When Dani got to "nobody ever asked me that," Ana said, very quietly, No. Nobody did.
Then she pulled the 2008 closing out of Phil's binder and read the last lines aloud.

Trial transcript, Monday, June 9, 2008, the prosecution's closing argument, excerpt. What she saw was a man in a red jacket strike Travis Hensley at a quarter past eleven and run. So who wore a red jacket that night? The defendant did. Put it together, and the man in the red jacket was Luis Ruiz.
Put it together, she said. That's the whole closing in three words. Of everything new since June of 2008, what hurts it most?

The cap, she tells her. Ronnie saw him go out bareheaded, and the man at the curb had one on. That's the one, Ana says. Not because it proves he wasn't there. Because she told them to put it together, and now there's a piece that doesn't go. She writes BAREHEADED 10:45, GALVAN under CAP, and dates it.

Strengthen or weaken a passage claim. The closing claims the pieces add up to Luis. A cap on the attacker, set beside a sighting of Luis bareheaded thirty minutes earlier, is a piece that points the other way, and the jury heard neither half.
Ana unzipped the freezer bag, slowly, and took out the notebook. I read this page Thursday and didn't know what it was for. She found it without hunting and turned it around.

Gene Vigil's notebook, Sunday, October 28, 2007, page four. A quarter past ten. R. Galvan, 30. Bartender, Night Owl. At his apartment, just woke up. Same as he gave Archuleta. Ruiz swung first, about ten twenty five. Hit the victim in the face. Didn't see what started it. Looked up at yelling. The victim had beer down his front. Knows Ruiz six or seven years. Likes him. Upset telling it. Good witness. If he's shading it, it's toward Ruiz. Ruiz out the back about a quarter to eleven.
Gene had it Sunday morning, Ana said. Didn't see what started it. Five hours before he sat down with your father.
Forget what you'd say about Ronnie. What would Gene say, from this page?
That a witness who likes the man he's describing is more believable when it hurts him.
If he's shading it, it's toward Ruiz, Ana reads. Gene believed Ronnie because Ronnie didn't want it to be true. So do I, for what it's worth. So did I in 2010.

Would agree with. "Likes him. Upset telling it," and then, "If he's shading it, it's toward Ruiz." Gene reasons that a witness who's sorry to say a thing is more credible for saying it. That's on the page, very nearly stated.

Tuesday night, on the drive home, her phone had lit up with a Northglenn number. It's Gene. Brennan's letter had come. He'd swear to the notebook any day she named. Then: Galvan called me Monday night. First time in years. You saw him. Monday. He threw up in the courthouse lot after he testified. Behind my car. I held his coffee. A pause. I drove the Buick to church Sunday. First time. She'd have laughed at me, how slow I took the turns.

Wednesday, January 20, seven. On her way down she stepped off the bottom stair into cold water, through her sock. A dark tongue of it ran out from under the washer across the concrete. She sat two steps up, wet foot and all, as the recording started.
Bishop out, he said. Right up next to your knight. Then: Furnace holding? Teo fixed it in October. I know who fixed it.
She told him she'd been to see Ronnie Galvan. The hiss. Ronnie. He still pouring? He's got a taqueria. Good for him. He always wanted that.
Pa. He says you swung first.

It came back fast, like it had been waiting at the front of his mouth for nineteen years. Ronnie was pouring four deep. Everybody was pushing. It was a World Series. I never hit that man, mija. I never touched him.
His blood was on your cuff, Pa. How did it get there if you never touched him?

The hiss goes on. Everybody was bleeding on everybody, he says finally. It was a bar. It's an answer that gives up more than it says. If everybody was bleeding on everybody, there was a fight. She doesn't say so. She hears him hear it.

Weaken. Physical evidence is the hardest thing for "I never touched him" to absorb. Travis's blood on his sleeve needs contact to get there, and the denial leaves no room for contact. It doesn't show what happened in the lot. It shows the denial can't be right as he states it.

He'd made her give him her move before they hung up. A pawn, pushed up at his bishop. She'd moved it on her own board with her wet foot on the step and hadn't felt it. I still have her two pages, he'd said at the end, like it had just come to him. Brennan's. I keep them with your mother's letters. Then the minute was up.

Thursday, January 21, two tamales sat on a paper plate on Dani's side of Ana's desk. The woman downstairs makes them Thursdays. I bought four. I don't eat four. She didn't look up from what she was writing. Dani ate both.
Line three on the board. 3. "THE GUY FROM THE BAR" WAS LUIS. Ana put the cap back on the marker and tapped the line with it.
Shannon's phone call. Their reading is that 'the guy' meant your father. What hurts that reading most?
Ronnie says Travis spent the whole game picking at Boston people. 'The guy' could be any of them.
Ana writes MOUTHING OFF SINCE THE 3RD next to line three. Their reading needs one guy. Now it's a bar full of guys with a reason. That's the sentence I want Meredith to have to answer.

Weaken. The State reads "the guy from the bar" as the man Travis fought because he was the only man Travis had trouble with. Evidence that Travis had trouble with others gives the phrase other men to point at. That's exactly the weak point.
Ana drew the timeline along the bottom edge of the board in pencil, in handwriting so small Dani had to stand up to read it. 10:25 FIGHT. 10:45 OUT THE BACK. 11:04 CALL. 11:15 ATTACK. 11:17 911.
Between the 10:45 and the 11:04 she wrote GONE BEFORE 11:04? Then she stood with the pencil an inch off the board, and Dicta, who could always tell when nobody was moving, lifted her head to check.
That's what we'd like to say. Right now it's only what he says, and what he says proves what he says. One fact. If it walked in that door tomorrow, which one helps that line most?
Anything with a clock on it that had him somewhere else before 11:04. A receipt. A tape.

That's my whole wish list in one sentence, Ana says. She writes RECORD? under the question mark and taps it twice. Nobody had one in 2008. Ask him where he went after that door. Not what he did. Where he went.

Strengthen. A record with a time and a place does what testimony can't. It puts him somewhere else with nobody's memory in between. If it's near 11:04 and far enough from the lot, the call came while he was gone, and getting back to the curb by 11:15 gets hard. It doesn't prove he wasn't there. It makes the line on the board much safer.
She'd texted Teo Thursday night. Basement floor's wet by the washer. He didn't answer. Sunday, January 24, at ten in the morning he was at the back door with a shop vac and his headlamp.

He lay on a flattened box with his head under the tub, swearing at it in a friendly way. Tub seal. It's weeping out the bottom. He slid out and lay there a second with the headlamp aimed at the joists. That's not a part, Dani. That's a whole washer. She told him it worked fine. It works on your floor. He sat up. The lamp swung across the shelf where the banker's box used to be. She'd carried it upstairs in December. He clicked it off. Not a word.

She told him about Ronnie over the vac, too loud. He shut it off mid sentence. Down there you could hear the furnace tick. The bartender, he said, and when she asked if he remembered him, Pa talked about him. Nothing else. He wound the cord over his elbow and around his hand, over and under, every loop the same size. Then, still winding: Maybe Pa had a reason. She said he couldn't know that. You can't know he didn't.

A minute later, mostly to the cord: Guy who did it ran, right? On foot. Pa didn't walk to the mailbox, he said. Pa drove to the end of the block for milk and left it running. If he'd done something out there he'd have been in that truck and gone. That's all I'm saying.

It was the most he'd said about that night in ten years, and he'd said it to a shop vac. She put it in Ana's order in her head, conclusion last: the man ran off on foot, Pa had his truck right there, men with trucks drive, so the man who ran probably wasn't Pa. She already knew Ana's next question, what would make that hold, and she answered it out loud.
That there's no road for a truck north of the lot where he ran. Just a ditch.
Then he wasn't running to a truck, Teo says. If that's what's out there. He goes back to the cord. She writes DITCH? MAP on the back of her hand in pen, and he watches her do it, and doesn't ask.

Strengthen. The weak point is that a man might run on foot to a truck parked somewhere else. If there was nowhere north for a truck to be, the man wasn't running to one. That closes off the one route by which "on foot" could still fit a man who'd driven there.
Wednesday, January 27, seven. She sat two steps up from the bottom now. Teo's shop vac stood by the washer, and every morning the concrete under the tub had a dark edge again, whatever she told it.
Recording first. Then, no hello: Bishop takes your knight.
The board sat on the step beside her, where it sat every Wednesday. She lifted her knight off and put his bishop on its square. Either of two pawns could take it back. A child could see it.

He didn't ask about the furnace. He didn't ask about anything. First Wednesday in ten years he didn't ask, in any of his ways. She waited for it. It didn't come. So she asked hers, the one on the bottom of Ana's board, flat, in Ana's voice. Pa. When you left that night. Did you stop anywhere? No. Not for gas. Nothing. Straight home, mija. I told you.
He'd told her. He'd told everybody. Your move, he said.
She had the knight in her hand. Next week, she said.
The line hissed. You never think about it. I'm thinking about it. A long breath on his end. Okay.
The lady came on to say there was one minute left. Neither of them used it.

Upstairs, after, she took the envelope out of the prep book at the kitchen table. MAYBE HE DID IT across the top, NEEDED and ENOUGH under it. Under her own capitals, in smaller ones, she wrote HE SWUNG FIRST.
Then one more line, smaller still, because Ana would have stood over her till she did. THAT'S ALL RONNIE SAW.

Thursday, January 28, Bianca dropped Lupe off at half past five, on her way to work. Teo had a bus down on Colfax. He'll get her by eight thirty. She's had a snack. She'll tell you she hasn't. On the porch she turned back. He was out in the truck again Sunday night. First time since Christmas. She looked at Dani as if Dani might know why. Dani had told him about Ronnie on Sunday. She didn't say so.

Lupe found the board before her coat was off. The knight lay on its side next to it. That's my horse. That's Grandpa's game. Why's it lying down? Grandpa took it. Lupe put her chin on the table, level with the pieces. She touched the pawn beside the bishop with one finger. Can't this one get him? It can. So get him back.
Dani didn't. Lupe gave her Teo's look and went back to drawing.

Teo came at twenty to nine, grease to the elbows, and stood in the doorway while Lupe told him everything, the snack she hadn't had, the horse, the pawn, and that Tía wouldn't. He looked down at the board. Their father had taught them both on the garage sale board at this table, with a salt shaker for a rook. Teo had been ten the last time he sat down to it.
He used to do that to me, he said. Do what? Give you something easy to take. So you're busy taking it. He zipped Lupe's coat to her chin. You quit looking at the rest of the board.
When they were gone she left his bishop on her knight's square and turned off the kitchen light.
